name: Valley Health
blurb: Two hospitals, nine clinics and 6,000 nurses and techs. Founder Dr. Evelyn Marsh built it from the Marrow Creek rural clinic, and her family trust holds 22% of the vote.

directors.name: Oliver Brandt
directors.title: Attorney
directors.motive: Your firm signed the compliance reports that missed this pattern, and Valley pays a third of your fees. Self-reporting puts your name on the first page of the filing. You would rather defend the coding as a reasonable reading and run the response yourself.

directors.name: Teresa Alvarado
directors.title: Labor director
directors.motive: Contract talks open in June, and a repayment of this size cuts nurse shifts before it cuts executives. You also promised the nurses who wrote the letter that something would change. You can back a leadership change, but not a $110 million check.

directors.name: Ruth Kessler
directors.title: Fund partner
directors.motive: Your fund owns 10% and your bonus rides on year-end value. Privately, the lender told you the covenant trips at $75 million of repayment but it would accept a three-year plan. A quiet fix looks safest to you, unless a lump sum is forced.

directors.name: Dr. Arthur Penn
directors.title: Founder's friend
directors.home: Dr. Evelyn Marsh, the founder (residency classmate)
directors.motive: Dr. Marsh gave you this seat, and her office hired the consultant. Self-reporting sends agents to her office first, and putting her on leave ends her career. You want the coding defended, or at least corrected without anyone being named.

directors.name: Imani Brooks
directors.title: Community seat
directors.motive: A reporter called you Monday about the nurses' letter, and you hold a hospital board seat for rural patients who drive two hours to Valley. You would rather Valley say it first, even at a cost, than read it in the paper.

directors.name: Gloria Feng
directors.title: Audit chair
directors.motive: Your committee reviewed the coding reports and the CFO told you they tied out, but you never tested them. Outside reviewers would start with your approvals. An interim leader who reviews the CFO first looks better to you than an open audit.

briefing.intro: Valley Health is a regional system of two hospitals, nine clinics and 6,000 nurses and techs, built by Dr. Evelyn Marsh, who holds 6% of the stock. Federal agents served search warrants over Medicare billing last week, no charges are filed, and the board must decide tonight what Valley tells the government.
facts: An internal audit found that pneumonia cases coded into the higher-paying group rose from 11% to 34% in three years while patients did not get sicker. Two earlier Medicare contractor reviews of about thirty charts each found nothing.

The coding guidance came from a consultant hired by Dr. Marsh's office and paid a share of the added revenue, who called it aggressive but defensible. The overpayment may be $40 million to $110 million, and no one has checked individual charts.
Valley keeps a second, internal cost report that does not match the one it filed with Medicare. Counsel says there may be legitimate reasons, and that agents will ask about the mismatch first.
Nurses sent the Chief Nursing Officer a letter saying they were pressured to code patients as sicker. It was filed, never reached the board, and a reporter called about it Monday.

Profit is about $180 million a year, so repaying $110 million would cut a year of earnings by more than half and could trip a bond covenant. Disclosing early may lower penalties, or it may not. The stock is $31, down from $36.

options.title: Self-report and repay
options.text: Tell Medicare now, offer repayment and bring in outside reviewers; the bill could reach $110 million and strain the bond covenant.

options.title: Correct guidance, answer questions
options.text: Change the coding guidance now and answer agents' questions as asked; the mismatched cost report may later look like concealment.

options.title: Contest the claims
options.text: Keep the guidance, call it an honest reading of unclear rules and hire litigators; fees run high and a cooperating doctor could change the case.

options.title: Leadership leave first
options.text: Put Dr. Marsh and the CFO on leave and let an interim leader decide; the government waits sixty days and Valley loses its founder.

reveal.text: The real firm was Columbia/HCA, then the largest US hospital chain. Federal agents served search warrants in 1997 and the investigation spread nationwide, and CEO Rick Scott resigned within months. Settlements through 2003, including upcoding of pneumonia diagnoses, brought recoveries of about $1.7 billion.

questions: Why did pneumonia coding jump from 11% to 34%?
The nurses' letter never reached the board. Who failed?
Regulators sometimes reward early disclosure and sometimes do not. Would you repay before anyone checks the charts, and what would change your answer?
Which option did you vote for, and what tipped it?

press.headline: Valley Health Reports Its Own Billing Pattern to Medicare
press.story: The board said it will repay once a sample chart review is done, with outside counsel reporting to directors. Analysts warned that a repayment near the top of the range would breach the bond covenant, and the nurses' union said shift cuts are under discussion at both hospitals.

press.headline: Valley Health Rewrites Coding Rules and Answers Questions as Asked
press.story: Valley changed its guidance and told agents only what they asked. Lenders were relieved that no repayment is planned, but the regional paper says the nurses' letter and a second cost report are the next questions.

press.headline: Valley Health Calls Billing Pattern an Honest Reading of Unclear Rules
press.story: The board kept its consultant and hired litigators. Lenders were relieved that no repayment is planned, but a lawyer for one of Valley's doctors is said to be talking to the agents.

press.headline: Valley Health Founder and Finance Chief Placed on Leave
press.story: An interim leader will run the system and decide what to disclose after a sixty-day review. Investors welcomed the break but asked why the government must wait two months, and several senior doctors said they are considering leaving with the founder.
